problem: FM-based embodied navigation agents suffer from training bias (poor personalization to unseen environments, e.g. objects that move with human habits) and from limited context length that hurts long-horizon tasks, especially on small on-device models.
motivation: Robots must work out-of-the-box in new homes, yet FMs lack scene-specific human habit knowledge and cannot hold long observation histories; large FMs also exceed on-device compute. Priming with mined habit data and actively filtering memory are cheap, fine-tuning-free ways to improve deployability.
key_idea: Prime the FM with learned object-transit (human-habit) models for personalized target finding (TAP), and add a detachable trainable 'memory head' (MemCtrl) on a frozen MLLM that decides which observations to keep or discard.
insight: Adding any memory head variant improves EB-ALFRED and EB-Habitat results over the plain Qwen2.5-VL-7B baseline, with the largest gains on Long and Complex instruction subsets (e.g. Habitat Long 2 -> 14 with offline supervised head), while using roughly half the context. TAP gains are largest in routine scenarios where paths have structure (57.5 -> 80.0), showing that habit priors help when entropy is low. This is a short position paper with small evaluation sets, so the evidence is suggestive.
method: Taxonomy: FM as Perceiver / Task Planner / Policy, with the limitations of each category.

Dynamic Object Maps (DOMs): convert topological scene graphs from real-world environments into dynamic node-attributed graphs simulating object transit under Static/Random/Semi-Routine/Fully-Routine scenarios (real2sim).
Transit model T / TAP: learn a human-habit model on DOM data and use it to prime the LLM planner (TAP-LLM) for finding portable objects, without fine-tuning the FM.
MemCtrl memory head μ: a detachable binary classifier on the frozen MLLM's latent embeddings that decides whether each observation is stored in or discarded from memory.

MemCtrl variants: Simple (query the MLLM directly about storage, untrained), Offline Supervised (trained on GPT-4o expert keep/discard labels), Online RL (policy trained with sparse task-success reward and dense action-success reward).

setting.backbone: TAP: LLM (following LGX) primed with transit model; MemCtrl: Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct (frozen) + trained memory head; GPT-4o as expert/baseline
setting.training_data: TAP: DOM simulated transit data from the lab scene (real2sim); MemCtrl: GPT-4o expert labels (offline supervised) or online RL interaction in EmbodiedBench; no FM fine-tuning
setting.observation: egocentric RGB images (plus text instruction); topological scene graph from lab images for TAP
setting.action_space: TAP: topological graph node navigation; MemCtrl: EmbodiedBench high-level discrete actions
setting.simulator: EmbodiedBench (EB-ALFRED, EB-Habitat); real-world Turtlebot lab environment
setting.privileged: none (TAP uses habit data mined from the scene in advance)

numbers.extra: online RL trained head; mean of 3 trials

numbers.eval_set_note: 50 episodes on a Turtlebot in lab; SR reported per scenario
numbers.extra: habit data mined from scene; scenarios Random/Semi-Routine/Routine

numbers_note: Baseline Qwen2.5-VL-7B (Avg 5.2 ALFRED, 15.2 Habitat) and the Simple variant are not listed as own methods; values are given in the table. Paper doesn't report standard navigation benchmarks.
results: TAP-LLM improves real-world SR over the vanilla LLM (LGX-style) in all scenarios (50.0/65.0/80.0 vs 37.5/45.0/57.5), about 18% on average. MemCtrl gives about 6% average gain on EmbodiedBench (Habitat Avg 15.2 -> 21.0; ALFRED 5.2 -> 9.8) and about 20% on long-instruction subsets with about half the context.
limitations: Small-scale, preliminary evaluation (50 real-world episodes in one lab; 3 trials on EmbodiedBench with low absolute success rates)
TAP relies on pre-mined habit data and a real2sim replica of the scene; MemCtrl needs expert labels or RL training per backbone
Behavioral differences between RL and offline heads are not analysed; the paper is largely a position/overview piece
